claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially exists as a high-temperature single-phase BCC alloy.
Cooling from the high-temperature BCC state produces nanoscale local chemical-order clusters.
The proposed local chemical order arises from uneven elemental partitioning during cooling.
The elevated Cr concentration is a particularly important driver of local chemical-order formation.
Slow cooling or intermediate-temperature holding permits more diffusion and local ordering than rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching strongly suppresses local chemical-order formation.
Local chemical-order regions modify local interfacial energies.
Local chemical-order regions lower the nucleation barrier for secondary phases.
During subsequent thermal exposure, local chemical-order clusters catalyze transformation of the uniform BCC state into a phase mixture.
Thermally evolving nanoscale chemical heterogeneities can govern material behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Slow-cooled samples will contain more nanoscale chemical ordering than rapidly quenched samples after otherwise identical thermal exposure.
Slow-cooled samples will exhibit a higher prevalence of secondary phases than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will preferentially retain the metastable BCC structure and a more homogeneous phase distribution.
The brittleness or ductility associated with the evolved structure depends on the degree or configuration of local chemical order.
Segregation and precipitation of brittle phases can promote brittle fracture in conventional alloys.
The proposed mechanism should cease to dominate when diffusion is suppressed or when non-diffusive transformation mechanisms dominate.
